item.lead: The corpus is now one long string, and the script cuts it in two with ordinary slicing. Look at the two lines that build the pieces: both use the same index, written the same way. Here is the same cut on a ten-character string, small enough to check by eye.
item.follow: The index in the first slice is where the second slice begins. A slice stops just before its end index, and the next slice starts exactly at it. So every character lands in one piece only, and none is dropped. Next: why the held-back piece must never be seen during training.

perform.line: /code Write a Python example that splits a string at one index into a first piece and a second piece. Use these sizes and values: data = 'abcdefghij', n = len(data), cut = int(n*0.9), train = data[:int(n*0.9)], val = data[int(n*0.9):]. Standard library and numpy only; nothing imported from the source. One comment per step, in the words the reader already knows: string, characters, index, slice, train piece, held-back piece. Steps: set the string and its length; slice the first piece up to the index; slice the second piece from the same index; print both pieces; print that train + val equals data and that the lengths add up to n, so no character is shared or missing. Do not print or state any output.
